query: Casting is the predominant fabrication method for high-entropy alloys, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can cause heterogeneous properties. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy compositions have reported high hardness and notable compressive performance, yet these findings do not establish how to improve CoCrFeNiTi; moreover, some investigated alloys were brittle at 25 °C and displayed only limited plastic deformation at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure, favorable plasticity and machinability, but low hardness and load-bearing capability, what single intervention could improve hardness and mechanical performance while preserving those favorable characteristics and clarifying the relationship between microstructure and deformation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the unmodified alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Grain refinement via rapid solidification can improve the hardness and mechanical performance of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys while preserving favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with a simple crystal structure
generation.conditions: Wheel speed adjusted to control undercooling levels
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain size and formation of twin boundaries
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary sliding and twinning accommodate deformation, leading to improved strength and ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved hardness and mechanical performance, with a predicted ultimate tensile strength of up to 2.5 GPa and hardness up to 300 MPa
generation.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with low hardness and load-bearing capability
generation.boundary: Grain size and twin boundary density influenced by wheel speed and undercooling levels
generation.uncertainty: Optimal wheel speed and undercooling levels for achieving desired microstructure and mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of mechanical properties of rapidly solidified CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with as-cast alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If rapidly solidified alloy does not exhibit improved hardness and mechanical performance compared to as-cast alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

Microstructure refinement and enhanced mechanical properties in rapid-quenched MnCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained significant attentions in recent years, due to their unique properties derived from the combination of multiple elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The mechanical properties of HEAs are influenced by microstructural characteristics. In this study, MnCrFeCoNi HEA ribbons were produced using a technique called melt spinning, for which the wheel speed was adjusted to control the undercooling levels. The rapid solidification process under undercooling condition resulted in refined grain sizes to micrometers in the ribbons. One notable feature was the appearance of twin boundaries, which especially accounted for approximately 7.36 % of the microstructure for the ribbons produced at a wheel speed of 10 m/s. For the ribbons with thickness of micrometer scale, the mechanical properties (ultimate tensile strength up to 2.5 GPa and hardness up to 300 MPa) were analyzed by microstructure (grain boundaries and homogeneity) and exterior factors (e.g. thickness). Microstructure and composition dependence of mechanical characteristics of nanoimprinted AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Molecular dynamics is applied to explore the deformation mechanism and crystal structure development of the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys under nanoimprinting. The influences of crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance on the mechanical properties are carefully analyzed. The imprinting load indicates that the highest loading force is in ascending order with polycrystalline, nano-twinned (NT) polycrystalline, and monocrystalline. The change in alloy composition suggests that the imprinting force increases as the Al content in the alloy increases. The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs). The deformation behavior shows that shear strain and local stress are concentrated not only around the punch but also on GBs and adjacent to GBs.
